Knell

/NEL/ - rhymes with bell · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Knell means the solemn sound of a bell, often indicating a death.

The convent bell rang a slow knell at dawn, and the town understood that the eldest sister had died in the night.

Worked Example

When the council voted to close the village school, the chairman said he heard a knell in the word 'carried': a village that loses its school, he told the room, has heard the first bell of its own funeral.

A knell is not just any ringing — it is the slow, solemn bell that announces a death, and by extension any signal that something is finished. That is why English speaks of a 'death knell' for trades, laws, and eras.

How Knell Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

toll

toll: the slow, measured ringing itself, for any solemn purpose

chime

chime: a bell note with no weight — hours, doorbells, ice-cream trucks

Antonyms

peal

peal: quick, joyful ringing, for weddings and victories

fanfare

fanfare: a bright trumpet burst announcing something glad

How Strong Is It? — chime → toll → knell

chime vs. knell

chime vs. knell: A chime is far lighter than a knell — a bright note marking the hour or a visitor at the door.

toll vs. knell

toll vs. knell: A toll is milder than a knell — bells toll slowly for many solemn occasions, but a knell announces a death or an ending.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — knell

Root — knell: Old English cnyll, the stroke of a bell

Put it together

Put it together: There is nothing to peel off here: knell is Old English cnyll, the stroke of a bell, from a verb cnyllan, 'to ring.' The k was pronounced a thousand years ago — k'nell — and though the sound fell silent, the spelling keeps its ghost. The word never grew a family; it simply kept ringing.

Why there's no relative to spot

Why there's no relative to spot: Knell stands alone in modern English: its parent verb cnyllan died out, leaving no cousins to recognize. What survives instead is the phrase it anchors — the 'death knell' — which lets one Old English syllable go on announcing endings a millennium later.

Strength Check

Word Choice

formal / literary

Knell is the bell that announces a death — and, figuratively, any signal that something is over: the ruling sounded the knell for the old law. Chimes are neutral and peals are joyful; a knell only ever means an ending. Its unit-mate dirge is the song sung after the news; the knell is the bell that breaks it.
